Hi Barsha,

We cover genetic distances in our recent review (See Box 2 of http://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/abs/10.1094/PHYTO-12-16-0425-RVW).

In short, Prevosti's distance (aka simple mismatch, aka manhattan... there are MANY names for this distance) will give you the fraction of alleles at which two individuals differ. In the case of dominant markers, this is also the fraction of loci. Regardless of marker type, it also has the nice property of being equivalent to the squared Euclidean distance for haploids.

I've mentioned this before on this forum and in the documentation, but bitwise.dist() is for genlight objects. It will work with genind objects, but in the background it's just calling prevosti.dist() [1]. There are three functions that all do the same thing in poppr (diss.dist(), prevosti.dist(), and bitwise.dist()) [2, 3], and the only one that's truly different is bitwise.dist because it's optimized for data that's been coded as bits.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

This question is more appropriate for the adegenet forums since glPca() is an adegenet function, but since you're here:

The plots represent the eigenvalues (you can think of these as variance) for each principal component. The sum of these eigenvalues represents the total variance of the observed data. Knowing that, the proportion of variance observed is obtained by taking the sum of the fraction of variance:

> var_frac <- Kob_pca$eig/sum(Kob_pca$eig)
> signif(sum(var_frac[1:3]) * 100, 3)

You can see this in practice when you look at the source Rmarkdown document for that section: https://github.com/grunwaldlab/Population_Genetics_in_R/blob/master/gbs_analysis.Rmd#principal-components-analysis

A word of caution: you specified to retain 3 principal components for the analysis, but your plot shows that you probably want to retain 12 or 19 components.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

messages.subject_clean: [poppr] Is the "threshold" a fixed argument or an upper limit in a "threshold" series in the mlg.filter() ?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The threshold defines the limit of genetic distance at which individuals would be considered of a different multilocus lineage (according to the algorithm defined).

> In the first picture, "threshold = 0" and the return is "$THRESHOLDS =0", BUT  in the second picture, "threshold = 1" and the return is "$THRESHOLDS =0" .Why?

Technically, THRESHOLDS did not return "0"; it returned "numeric(0)", which indicates a zero-length numeric vector. In other words, no MLGs were collapsed.

Because mlg.filter() collapses MLGs into lineages, the output of mlg.filter(..., stats = "THRESHOLDS") gives all of the thresholds at which two MLGs were merged into a lineage. In this example, the smallest genetic distance > 0 is 1. Since this distance represents the lower limit to consider MLLs separate, only the two MLGs that had a 0 genetic distance were collapsed, hence THRESHOLDS == 0. If you had set "threshold = 1.1", you would have gotten 0 and 1 as the result.
Hope that helps,
Zhian

Hi Barsha,

The nodes of the MSN represent genotypes and the lines connecting them represent genetic distance between these genotypes. This is constructed to represent the minimum spanning tree that connects these nodes. In your graph, you can see that a few of the nodes are overlapping other nodes. These nodes are connected, but the nature of the plotting makes it difficult to know how. It should be noted that in the current version of poppr, the size of these nodes are skewed as they are scaled by radius (as opposed to area), so larger nodes will be artificially inflated. The next version of poppr will scale these nodes by area instead (you can install the development version from github to try it out https://github.com/grunwaldlab/poppr).
